subject: literature
topic: Drama: types (tragedy, comedy, tragicomedy, farce) and dramatic terms (soliloquy, aside, catharsis, hamartia)

kept.q: In a stage play, Chief Odion stands alone after his guests leave and says to himself, 'My son thinks I do not see his greed, but I built this empire and I shall decide who inherits it.' Which dramatic term best describes this speech?
options: Soliloquy
Aside
Monologue delivered to another character
Dramatic irony
kept.explanation: Because Chief Odion is alone on stage and speaking his private thoughts aloud, this is a soliloquy, not a remark directed at another character or the audience.
kept.pidgin: Because Chief Odion dey alone for stage dey talk im mind, na soliloquy be that. E no dey talk to another pesin or the audience.

kept.q: Which of these best defines 'farce' as a type of drama, distinguishing it from comedy of manners?
options: A play exposing the polished wit and social affectation of the upper class
A play relying on absurd coincidences, mistaken identities and knockabout physical action purely to provoke laughter
A serious play with a happy resolution after near-tragic events
A play in which a noble character falls due to a personal weakness
kept.explanation: Farce is built on exaggerated, improbable situations and physical comedy meant simply to entertain, unlike comedy of manners which satirises refined social behaviour.
kept.pidgin: Farce dey rely on funny, unbelievable situations and physical comedy just to make pipu laugh. E different from comedy of manners wey dey yab high-class social behaviour.

kept.q: During a performance, the character Sade turns briefly from her conversation with her sister and whispers to the audience, 'She has no idea I already sold the land,' before continuing the conversation as if nothing happened. This device is called:
options: Soliloquy
Aside
Flashback
Catharsis
kept.explanation: An aside is a short remark made to the audience (or another character) that other characters on stage are assumed not to hear, exactly as Sade's whisper functions here.
kept.pidgin: Aside na when pesin talk small secret to the audience or anoda pesin wey other pipu for stage no suppose hear. Na wetin Sade do be that.

kept.q: A dramatist writes a play in which a respected judge, convinced that his wealth makes him untouchable, bribes his way out of every scandal until a single case exposes him publicly, leading to his imprisonment and disgrace. Which element of tragedy is most clearly illustrated by the judge's downfall?
options: Comic relief
Hamartia arising from hubris
Dramatic exposition
Deus ex machina
kept.explanation: The judge's downfall results from his own flaw, an excessive belief in his untouchability, which is hamartia rooted in hubris, a classic tragic pattern.
kept.pidgin: The judge fall because of im own pride and belief say nobody fit touch am. Na classic hamartia and hubris be that.

kept.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes classical tragedy from tragicomedy?
options: Tragedy always ends in reconciliation while tragicomedy ends in death
Tragedy centres on the downfall of a noble figure through his own flaw, while tragicomedy blends serious danger with elements that allow a non-fatal or balanced resolution
Tragedy uses only comic characters while tragicomedy uses only serious ones
Tragedy has no moral lesson while tragicomedy always teaches a lesson
kept.explanation: Classical tragedy ends in the hero's ruin or death caused by a personal flaw, whereas tragicomedy mixes grave, tragedy-like situations with comic or redemptive elements that avert total disaster.
kept.pidgin: Tragedy dey end for hero ruin or death because of im own error, but tragicomedy dey mix serious danger with happy ending.

kept.q: In a play, a wealthy trader named Musa loses his business empire because he consistently refuses sound advice from his accountant, trusting only his own judgment even when figures clearly show looming bankruptcy. A student argues that Musa's stubborn self-reliance is his hamartia. Which additional evidence from the plot would most strongly support this claim?
options: Musa's business fails due to a sudden fire caused by an electrical fault
Musa ignores three separate warnings from people who later prove correct
A rival trader sabotages Musa's warehouse out of jealousy
The market experiences a general economic downturn affecting all traders
kept.explanation: Hamartia must arise from the character's own persistent flaw; repeatedly ignoring credible warnings shows the downfall stems from Musa's own judgment, not external accident or circumstance.
kept.pidgin: Hamartia must come from the pesin own personal flaw. Musa wey ignore warning three times show say na im own stubbornness cause im downfall.

kept.q: A travelling drama troupe in Ibadan stages a play in which the central character suffers severe family betrayal and near financial ruin, yet through a sudden fortunate discovery, all conflicts are resolved and the play ends with laughter and feasting. Which dramatic type best fits this description?
options: Pure tragedy
Tragicomedy
Comedy of manners
Farce
kept.explanation: The play mixes serious, near-tragic suffering with an eventual happy, comic resolution, which is the defining feature of tragicomedy rather than pure tragedy or farce.
kept.pidgin: As the play mix serious near-tragic suffer with happy ending, na tragicomedy be that, no be pure tragedy or farce.

kept.q: Which of the following best explains why catharsis is considered essential to Aristotle's concept of tragedy?
options: It allows the audience to laugh at the hero's misfortune
It provides comic relief that lightens the tragic mood
It enables the audience to emotionally release pity and fear, leaving them purified rather than merely distressed
It ensures the villain is punished at the end of the play
kept.explanation: Aristotle argued that tragedy's purpose is to arouse pity and fear in the audience and then purge these emotions, leaving a sense of relief rather than lingering distress, which is catharsis.
kept.pidgin: Catharsis mean say as the audience dey watch tragedy, pity and fear go enter dem body, and at last dem mind go pure and relieve.
